results.q: What caused the furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca?
results.text:
The furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca was caused by the inadvertent simultaneous opening of two motor-operated valves that were supposed to isolate Furnace 5. That opened a path for cracked gas to backflow into the furnace firebox, where lit pilots ignited it and caused the explosion. [monaca-037][monaca-015]

The CSB said several things contributed to that chain of events. Shell assigned a process control engineer with limited process knowledge to manipulate the valves. Shell also relied on ineffective administrative controls instead of engineered protection against backflow. And the valve-control human-machine interface was confusing: it put three similar valves on one screen without clear labels to distinguish them. [monaca-037][monaca-002]

The incident happened on June 4, 2025, at Shell Polymers Monaca in Pennsylvania. It damaged Furnace 5, led to a fire, and forced evacuation of 15 employees in the area. Shell estimated about $95 million in property damage. [monaca-001][monaca-017]

results.text:
Reactor 6’s relief system was inadequate because it was sized for the wrong scenario. The CSB said the system functioned as designed, but it was undersized for the accelerated sugar decomposition reaction that happened that day, so it could not relieve the gas and pressure fast enough. What set that up was a vent valve that failed closed, which blocked normal venting and let temperature and pressure rise. That accelerated the sugar ingredient’s decomposition, producing even more heat and carbon dioxide. The facility was not aware the sugar ingredient could react this way, so neither the cooling system nor the emergency relief system had been sized for this accelerated decomposition scenario. The CSB said the existing emergency pressure relief system would have needed to be four times larger, or a 4-inch rupture disc alone would have needed to provide the relief capacity. [givaudan-060][givaudan-035]

results.q: What do the PEMEX and Wacker incidents have in common?
results.text:
They had several things in common. In both incidents, a maintenance task on live hazardous equipment went wrong, and the CSB tied the event to weak work planning and weak control of the hazards around the job. [pemex-001][wacker-034]

In PEMEX, contractors opened the wrong piping during maintenance and released toxic hydrogen sulfide. In Wacker, a contractor over-torqued bolts on a live HCl flange connection, fractured piping, and released gaseous hydrogen chloride. Both incidents injured workers, and both involved contract crews working around hazardous process equipment. [pemex-001][wacker-001]

The CSB also pointed to similar system problems: lack of clear job-specific procedures, poor control of hazardous energy, and weak permit or work-control systems. In both cases, the company did not adequately make sure the workers understood the exact equipment and hazards before the work started. [pemex-002][pemex-048][wacker-033][wacker-034]

Another shared theme was that the work was happening in a busy area with other workers nearby, so the hazard spread beyond the crew doing the task. PEMEX exposed nearby contractors in an adjacent unit, and Wacker exposed other contractors on the fifth-floor platform because the company did not properly manage simultaneous work. [pemex-048][wacker-002]

So, in plain language: both were maintenance incidents where poor identification, poor planning, and poor coordination around hazardous live equipment helped turn a routine job into a release that hurt workers. [pemex-048][wacker-034]

results.q: What did the CSB conclude about the Evergreen Packaging incident?
results.text:
The CSB concluded that the Evergreen Packaging report was used as the basis for a later Wacker recommendation on simultaneous operations, or SIMOPs. In the Wacker report, the Board said the Evergreen Packaging recommendation to OSHA on coordinating SIMOPs was superseded and replaced with broader recommendations that apply to general industry and construction, not just confined space work. [wacker-003][wacker-035]

The Wacker report also said the Evergreen Packaging incident was one of several other CSB cases involving SIMOPs problems, where work crews that were not part of the initiating event were injured or killed because the simultaneous work was not properly coordinated. For Evergreen Packaging, the report says two contract companies were doing maintenance in connected process vessels when a heat gun ignited flammable resin, causing a fire and two fatalities. [wacker-025]
